front: A hydraulic lift multiplies force tenfold, so the input piston must move {{c1::ten times farther}}.
why: Hydraulic force-distance tradeoff via incompressibility; common Pascal follow-up

front: A submarine is at a depth of 100 m in seawater (ρ = 1025 $kg/m^{3}$). What is the gauge pressure? (g = 9.8 $m/s^{2}$)
why: Gauge pressure rho*g*h calculation; appears every year

front: A vessel narrows to half its radius at constant driving pressure. By what factor does flow drop?
why: Poiseuille r^4 numeric application (half radius, 1/16 flow)

front: An IV bag must hang high enough that {{c1::$\rho g h$}} exceeds {{c1::the patient's venous pressure}}.
why: IV bag height via rho*g*h vs venous pressure; classic clinical application

front: An object floats when its density is:
why: Float/sink by density comparison; foundational buoyancy fact

front: Blood has a specific gravity near 1.06, so its density is {{c1::about $1060$ kg/m$^3$}}.
why: Specific gravity definition with blood value; supporting detail

front: By Bernoulli's principle, where a fluid speeds up at constant height its pressure {{c1::decreases}}.
why: Bernoulli: faster flow, lower pressure; tested every year

front: Continuity or Poiseuille: which explains slow capillary flow, and which explains high resistance in a stenosis?
why: Continuity vs Poiseuille for capillaries vs stenosis; common circulation passage step

front: Does the buoyant force on a fully submerged object increase with depth?
why: Buoyancy independent of depth for incompressible fluid; classic conceptual

front: Give hydrostatic pressure with depth.
why: Hydrostatic pressure P=P0+rho*g*h; core fluids equation

front: Give the continuity equation.
why: Continuity equation A1v1=A2v2; used every year

front: How does absolute pressure at depth differ from gauge pressure?
why: Absolute vs gauge pressure distinction; needed on every pressure calculation

front: How does hydrostatic weighing determine body composition?
why: Hydrostatic weighing application; plausible passage context

front: How does raising hematocrit affect cardiac workload?
why: Hematocrit and viscosity in Poiseuille; secondary physiology link

front: How does vessel radius affect flow (Poiseuille)?
why: Poiseuille r^4 dependence; the qualitative Poiseuille fact tested every year

front: In Poiseuille's law, flow rate is proportional to {{c1::the fourth power of the radius}}.
why: Poiseuille r^4 cloze; restates the main Poiseuille card

front: Laplace's law for an alveolus gives $P = 2\gamma/r$. What does it predict?
why: Laplace's law for alveoli; respiratory physiology crossover

front: One mmHg is about {{c1::133 Pa}}, and atmospheric pressure is about {{c1::760 mmHg}}.
why: mmHg to Pa and 760 mmHg = 1 atm; unit conversion needed in clinical passages

front: Pressure in a static fluid depends on depth and density but not on {{c1::the shape or volume of the container}}.
why: Pressure independent of container shape; hydrostatic paradox is a common conceptual

front: State Archimedes' principle.
why: Archimedes' principle; on essentially every administration

front: State Bernoulli's principle.
why: Bernoulli's equation; core fluids equation

front: State Pascal's principle and its hydraulic consequence.
why: Pascal's principle and F1/A1=F2/A2; calculated every year

front: Surface tension arises from {{c1::cohesive forces between liquid molecules}} at an interface.
why: Surface tension origin; outline item but rarely more than context

front: The buoyant force equals the weight of {{c1::the fluid displaced}}, not the weight of the object.
why: Buoyant force equals displaced fluid weight; restates Archimedes card

front: Vascular resistance is {{c1::$8\eta L/(\pi r^4)$}}, so viscosity and length enter {{c1::linearly}}.
why: Resistance 8*eta*L/(pi*r^4); viscosity and length linear vs r^4

front: What distinguishes turbulent from laminar flow, and why does it matter clinically?
why: Turbulent vs laminar and Reynolds number; secondary qualitative detail

front: What four assumptions does Bernoulli's equation require?
why: Bernoulli assumptions; useful for understanding, rarely the tested point

front: What fraction of a floating object sits below the surface?
why: Submerged fraction equals density ratio; classic buoyancy calculation

front: What happens to pressure inside an arterial stenosis?
why: Pressure drop inside a stenosis; standard Bernoulli application

front: Which raises resistance more: halving a vessel's radius, or doubling its length?
why: Radius vs length effect on resistance; restates the Poiseuille cards

front: Why can a forced expiration collapse an airway (dynamic compression)?
why: Dynamic airway compression is respiratory-physiology detail

front: Why do stiletto heels damage a floor when flat shoes do not, if body weight is unchanged?
why: Pressure=F/A applied to heels; definition-level application

front: Why does a person float higher in salt water than in fresh water?
why: Floating higher in denser fluid; common Archimedes conceptual

front: Why does a person with a higher body fat fraction float more easily?
why: Restates float/sink by density using body-fat trivia

front: Why does an aneurysm tend to enlarge once it forms?
why: Aneurysm growth combines Bernoulli and Laplace; off-outline clinical detail

front: Why is arterial pressure higher in the feet than at the heart when standing?
why: Hydrostatic column adds rho*g*h to arterial pressure; common physiology application

front: Why is blood slowest in capillaries even though each capillary is tiny?
why: Capillary velocity via continuity; restates the continuity vs Poiseuille card

front: A $50.0$ cm$^3$ sample of olive oil has a mass of $46.0$ g. What are its density in SI units and its specific gravity?
why: Density and SG conversions feed every buoyancy and pressure calculation.

front: Absolute pressure is about $2$ atm at a depth of $10$ m in a freshwater lake, so at $30$ m it is about {{c1::$4$ atm}}.
why: Applying $P = P_0 + \rho g h$ to absolute pressure is tested on every MCAT.

front: A mercury barometer stands at $760$ mm. Filled with water instead, its column would be about {{c1::$10.3$ m}} tall.
why: Barometer column comparisons appear mainly as passage context.

front: In an open-tube U manometer, the liquid is pushed down on the {{c1::higher-pressure}} side, and the level difference gives $P - P_{\text{atm}} = \rho g \Delta h$.
why: Reading gauge pressure from a height difference recurs in pressure questions.

front: Intrapleural pressure is normally about $-4$ mmHg. What does the negative sign mean, and what is the absolute pressure at sea level?
why: Gauge vs absolute conversions, including negative gauge values, are commonly tested.

front: A hydraulic jack's output piston has $5$ times the input piston's diameter. What load can a $200$ N input force support?
why: Diameter-given hydraulic problems are a standard Pascal trap.

front: A rock weighs $50$ N in air and $40$ N when hung fully submerged in water. What is its specific gravity?
why: Apparent-weight SG problems are a common Archimedes application.

front: A floating object displaces its own {{c1::weight}} of fluid; a fully submerged object displaces its own {{c2::volume}} of fluid.
why: Core Archimedes reasoning tested on every MCAT.

front: A block floats in water with $60\%$ of its volume submerged. What fraction is submerged when it floats in oil of SG $0.8$?
why: Moving a floater between fluids is a common quantitative buoyancy question.

front: An object denser than oil but less dense than water is dropped into a beaker of oil floating on water. Where does it come to rest?
why: Two-fluid floating shows up mainly in passage or lab scenarios.

front: When an ice cube floating in a glass of water melts completely, the water level {{c1::stays the same}}.
why: Classic buoyancy conceptual question.

front: In a narrow glass tube, water forms a {{c1::concave}} meniscus and rises, while mercury forms a {{c2::convex}} meniscus and is depressed.
why: Capillary action is secondary content, usually seen in passages.

front: Normal urine specific gravity runs from about {{c1::$1.005$ to $1.030$}}.
why: The lesson marks the normal urine SG range as low-yield.

front: An infusion pump delivers $120$ mL/min through tubing of cross-sectional area $0.10$ cm$^2$. What is the saline's average speed?
why: Flow rate vs speed with unit conversion is a common discrete calculation.

front: Doppler shows blood speeding from $30$ to $270$ cm/s through a stenosis at unchanged flow, so the lumen radius is about {{c1::one-third}} of normal.
why: Continuity with the radius-squared step is tested on every MCAT.

front: Water flows at $1$ m/s through a horizontal pipe of area $10$ cm$^2$ into a throat of area $2$ cm$^2$. How much lower is the throat pressure, and what height difference do the Venturi tubes show?
why: The Venturi meter is a common continuity-then-Bernoulli application.

front: Water at $1$ m/s in a $6$ cm$^2$ pipe rises $2$ m into a $2$ cm$^2$ section. How much lower is the pressure in the upper section? ($g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
why: Full Bernoulli with speed and height changes is tested on every MCAT.

front: Liquid leaks from a small hole a depth $h$ below the surface of a wide open tank at speed {{c1::$v = \sqrt{2gh}$}}.
why: Torricelli's theorem is a frequently tested Bernoulli special case.

front: A pitot tube reads a stagnation pressure $250$ Pa above the static pressure in an air stream ($\rho = 1.25$ kg/m$^3$). What is the air speed?
why: Pitot tubes appear as passage-context applications of Bernoulli.

front: Cutting a vessel's radius by only about {{c1::16%}} halves its flow at a fixed pressure difference.
why: Poiseuille's $r^4$ dependence is tested on every MCAT.

front: Each capillary is narrower than an arteriole, so why is the largest systemic pressure drop across the arterioles?
why: Where pressure falls in the circulation is a commonly tested physics-physiology link.

front: After a leg amputation removes one parallel vascular bed, with cardiac output unchanged, what happens to TPR and MAP?
why: Series vs parallel vascular beds and $MAP = CO \times TPR$ are commonly tested.

front: For a stenosis, when does Bernoulli apply and when does Poiseuille?
why: Choosing the right law for a stenosis is a frequent passage question.

front: Name the three fluids regimes to identify first in a passage, with the tools for each.
why: Regime selection is the gateway step for fluids passages.

front: Why can severe anemia produce a heart murmur even with normal valves?
why: Reynolds-number reasoning appears mainly in clinical passages.
